power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objectives: Rest-activity rhythm organization and social interaction have each been linked to late-life depression, yet their independent longitudinal contributions have rarely been examined within a framework separating between-person differences from within-person fluctuations.
This study examined their independent associations with depressive symptoms in communitydwelling older adults.
Method: Data from Rounds 12-14 (2022-2024) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) included 1,532 person-wave observations from 606 participants.
text.formatted: Method: Data from Rounds <ref type="formula">12-14 (2022-2024</ref>) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) included 1,532 person-wave observations from 606 participants.

text.text: A Behavioral Rhythm Index (BRI) combined mean activity, relative amplitude, and reversed day-to-day variability.
Person-mean-centered random-intercept linear mixed models separated within-from between-person associations, adjusting for wave, age, sex, and education.

Results: Higher BRI was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = -0.238, p < .001) and within persons (B = -0.139, p = .013), although the within-person association was not robust across sensitivity analyses.
text.formatted: Results: Higher BRI was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = -0.238, p < .001) and within persons (B = -0.139, p = .013), although the within-person association was not robust across sensitivity analyses.

text.text: Greater social interaction was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = -0.714, p < .001) but not within persons.
text.formatted: Greater social interaction was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = -0.714, p < .001) but not within persons.

text.text: BRI and social interaction did not significantly interact (χ²(2) = 2.05, p = .359).

Conclusion: Higher BRI and greater habitual social engagement were each independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms between individuals, warranting further investigation as potentially modifiable behavioral factors in late-life depression.
The United States population aged 65 and older is projected to reach 82 million by 2050, comprising nearly one in four Americans (Population Reference Bureau, 2024).
text.formatted: The United States population aged 65 and older is projected to reach 82 million by 2050, comprising nearly one in four Americans <ref type="bibr">(Population Reference Bureau, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Late-life depression is a pressing public health concern within this growing demographic.

Depressive symptoms in older adults are associated with functional decline, disability, greater healthcare utilization, and elevated mortality risk (Fiske et al., 2009), with prevalence estimates ranging from 15% to 27% among community-dwelling individuals (Zivin et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Depressive symptoms in older adults are associated with functional decline, disability, greater healthcare utilization, and elevated mortality risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Fiske et al., 2009)</ref>, with prevalence estimates ranging from 15% to 27% among community-dwelling individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Zivin et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Late-life transitions such as retirement, bereavement, and functional decline frequently disrupt established daily routines, and disruption of behavioral regularity has been linked to mood instability and depressive symptomatology across the lifespan (Monk et al., 1991).
text.formatted: Late-life transitions such as retirement, bereavement, and functional decline frequently disrupt established daily routines, and disruption of behavioral regularity has been linked to mood instability and depressive symptomatology across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Monk et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Social rhythm theory provides a theoretical framework for this link.

Recurring social and behavioral events serve as zeitgebers that entrain circadian rhythms; when these anchors are disrupted, biological dysregulation follows and mood suffers (Ehlers et al., 1988; Frank et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Recurring social and behavioral events serve as zeitgebers that entrain circadian rhythms; when these anchors are disrupted, biological dysregulation follows and mood suffers <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ehlers et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Frank et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Two features of daily life are thus jointly implicated: the organization of rest-activity patterns, which reflects how consistently the body cycles through active and rest states, and participation in social activities, which provides interpersonal cues that stabilize those rhythms (Ehlers et al., 1988).
text.formatted: Two features of daily life are thus jointly implicated: the organization of rest-activity patterns, which reflects how consistently the body cycles through active and rest states, and participation in social activities, which provides interpersonal cues that stabilize those rhythms <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ehlers et al., 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Social rhythm theory also provides a rationale for examining whether restactivity organization and social engagement jointly relate to depressive symptoms, though the nature and direction of such interplay remain uncertain.
Wrist-worn accelerometers enable objective quantification of rest-activity rhythm organization in large community samples (Luik et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Wrist-worn accelerometers enable objective quantification of rest-activity rhythm organization in large community samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Luik et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Activity volume, circadian amplitude, and day-to-day variability were combined into a multidimensional behavioral composite to capture complementary aspects of daily activity patterns, and disrupted rest-activity patterns have been linked to depression and poorer psychological well-being in older adults (Authors, 2026; Luik et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Activity volume, circadian amplitude, and day-to-day variability were combined into a multidimensional behavioral composite to capture complementary aspects of daily activity patterns, and disrupted rest-activity patterns have been linked to depression and poorer psychological well-being in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Authors, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Luik et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Social interaction is likewise independently associated with depressive symptoms, loneliness, and cognitive decline in this population (Santini et al., 2020), with social activities buffering mood through positive reinforcement, reduced rumination, and maintenance of social identity and purpose (Martell et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Social interaction is likewise independently associated with depressive symptoms, loneliness, and cognitive decline in this population <ref type="bibr">(Santini et al., 2020)</ref>, with social activities buffering mood through positive reinforcement, reduced rumination, and maintenance of social identity and purpose <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Martell et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Yet few studies have jointly examined objectively measured rest-activity organization and social engagement as longitudinal correlates of depressive symptoms in older adults.
A critical methodological obstacle further limits existing research.

Few studies have distinguished whether older adults who habitually maintain more organized routines or greater social engagement report fewer depressive symptoms (a stable between-person difference) from whether the same individual reports fewer symptoms during waves when their own routine is more structured or their social participation is higher than usual (a within-person association) (Curran & Bauer, 2011).
text.formatted: Few studies have distinguished whether older adults who habitually maintain more organized routines or greater social engagement report fewer depressive symptoms (a stable between-person difference) from whether the same individual reports fewer symptoms during waves when their own routine is more structured or their social participation is higher than usual (a within-person association) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Curran & Bauer, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These are distinct questions with distinct implications: within-person associations suggest dynamic covariation that may reflect modifiable processes, whereas between-person associations may reflect enduring differences in health, resources, or social circumstances (Curran & Bauer, 2011).
text.formatted: These are distinct questions with distinct implications: within-person associations suggest dynamic covariation that may reflect modifiable processes, whereas between-person associations may reflect enduring differences in health, resources, or social circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Curran & Bauer, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Conflating these levels of analysis risks misattributing stable individual traits as dynamic processes amenable to intervention (Luik et al., 2013; Santini et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Conflating these levels of analysis risks misattributing stable individual traits as dynamic processes amenable to intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Luik et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Santini et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The present study addresses these gaps.

Using three annual waves of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS; Freedman & Kasper, 2019), a nationally representative longitudinal cohort of U.S. adults aged 65 and older, we applied person-mean-centered multilevel models to simultaneously estimate between-person and within-person associations of rest-activity rhythm organization and social interaction with depressive symptoms.
text.formatted: Using three annual waves of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Freedman & Kasper, 2019)</ref>, a nationally representative longitudinal cohort of U.S. adults aged 65 and older, we applied person-mean-centered multilevel models to simultaneously estimate between-person and within-person associations of rest-activity rhythm organization and social interaction with depressive symptoms.

text.text: Three pre-specified objectives were examined: (1) whether between-person differences in the Behavioral Rhythm Index (BRI) and social interaction are independently associated with depressive symptoms; (2) whether within-person fluctuations in BRI and social interaction are associated with concurrent depressive symptoms; and (3) whether BRI and social interaction interact in their associations with depressive symptoms at both levels of analysis.

Data were drawn from Rounds 12, 13, and 14 (2022-2024) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), a nationally representative longitudinal cohort of Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 years and older (Freedman & Kasper, 2019).
text.formatted: Data were drawn from Rounds 12, 13, and 14 (2022-2024) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), a nationally representative longitudinal cohort of Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 years and older <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Freedman & Kasper, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: NHATS employs a complex, stratified probability sampling design anchored to the Medicare enrollment file, with annual data collection through structured in-person interviews and, since Round 11, an accelerometer substudy.
The study protocol was approved by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health Institutional Review Board (IRB No. 00002083), and all participants provided informed consent.
Person-wave data across Rounds 12-14 were linked using unique NHATS participant identifiers to form a long-format repeated-measures dataset.
Participants were included when they contributed at least one wave with four or more valid accelerometer days.
The pooled accelerometry dataset comprised 1,642 person-wave observations from 633 unique participants (Round 12: n = 630; Round 13: n = 536; Round 14: n = 476).

Although NHATS enrolls adults aged 65 and older, the youngest age category represented in this accelerometer subsample was 70-74 years, reflecting that the accelerometer sub-study began in Round 11 and that younger enrollees were less likely to have accumulated the required number of valid accelerometer days by Round 12.

Age and wave are also partly entangled in this cohort: the 70-74 age group decreased from 16.0% at Round 12 to approximately 2% by Round 14, as this cohort ages, which should be considered when interpreting the wave coefficient.

The primary complete-case multilevel analysis included 1,532 observations from 606 participants; a sensitivity analysis using the six-item social interaction measure included 1,048 observations from 434 participants.
Baseline education was linked from Round 12 by participant identifier.

Of the 1,642 pooled person-wave observations, 110 were excluded from the primary analysis due to missing data on PHQ-2 (n = 73 person-waves), education (n = 36), or social interaction (n = 3), yielding the complete-case sample of 1,532 person-waves from 606 participants.
Missing-data categories were not mutually exclusive; some person-wave observations had missing values on more than one variable.
At Round 12 baseline, excluded observations (n = 40 participants) were older, more likely to be female (62.5% vs.
53.9%), and had higher mean depressive symptom scores (M = 0.86 vs.
0.64) compared with included participants.

Because the analytic sample is defined by accelerometer participation and data availability, NHATS survey weights were not applied; estimates describe associations within the analytic sample rather than population-representative parameters.
Wrist-worn accelerometer minute-level activity data were processed separately for each round (Karas et al., 2021; Schrack et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Wrist-worn accelerometer minute-level activity data were processed separately for each round <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Karas et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Schrack et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Days flagged as valid in the NHATS accelerometry files were retained if at least 80% of minute observations were non-missing (Schrack et al., 2022); participants contributed at least four valid days per wave.
text.formatted: Days flagged as valid in the NHATS accelerometry files were retained if at least 80% of minute observations were non-missing <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Schrack et al., 2022)</ref>; participants contributed at least four valid days per wave.

text.text: Mean activity volume was computed as the participant's mean across valid days.
The lowest five-hour (L5) and highest ten-hour (M10) windows were identified circularly across the 24-hour clock.

Relative amplitude (RA) was calculated as (M10 -L5) / (M10 + L5) (Van Someren et al., 1999), and the coefficient of variation (CV) was the standard deviation of daily mean activity divided by its mean.
text.formatted: Relative amplitude (RA) was calculated as (M10 -L5) / (M10 + L5) <ref type="bibr">(Van Someren et al., 1999)</ref>, and the coefficient of variation (CV) was the standard deviation of daily mean activity divided by its mean.

text.text: Mean activity, RA, and reversed CV were each z-standardized across the pooled Rounds 12-14 person-wave dataset; the BRI was their arithmetic mean.
Higher BRI reflects greater activity volume, stronger day-night contrast, and lower day-to-day variability.

The three BRI indicators were treated as formative components capturing different dimensions of activity behavior, so internal-consistency coefficients were not used as evidence of scale reliability (Bollen & Lennox, 1991).
text.formatted: The three BRI indicators were treated as formative components capturing different dimensions of activity behavior, so internal-consistency coefficients were not used as evidence of scale reliability <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bollen & Lennox, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: A component-level sensitivity model examined their separate associations.

Social interaction was assessed using four self-reported NHATS items: visiting friends or family in person, attending religious services or group meetings, participating in clubs or organized activities, and engaging in volunteer or community work.
Items were binary-coded (0 = did not participate,1 = participated) and averaged to a composite score (range 0-1), with higher scores indicating greater engagement.
A sensitivity analysis used a six-item version that additionally included going out for enjoyment and use of social networking sites.
Depressive symptoms were measured with the PHQ-2 (Kroenke et al., 2003), comprising two items assessing depressed mood and anhedonia over the past two weeks.
text.formatted: Depressive symptoms were measured with the PHQ-2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Kroenke et al., 2003)</ref>, comprising two items assessing depressed mood and anhedonia over the past two weeks.

text.text: NHATS administers these items on a three-point scale (1 = not at all;2 = several days;3 = more than half the days or nearly every day), collapsing the two highest frequency categories from the standard four-point format.
Each item was recoded 0-2 and summed, yielding scores ranging from 0 to 4, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.

Models adjusted for sex (female vs. male), wave (coded 0, 1, 2 for Rounds 12-14), age category (70-74 years [reference], 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, and ≥90 years), and education (fivelevel nominal factor: less than high school [reference], high school/GED, some college, college, and graduate education).
BRI and social interaction were decomposed following the within-between random-effects specification (Bell et al., 2019; Curran & Bauer, 2011).
text.formatted: BRI and social interaction were decomposed following the within-between random-effects specification <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Curran & Bauer, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: For each time-varying predictor, the between-person component was each participant's mean across all available waves; the withinperson component was the wave-specific deviation from that mean.
This approach permits simultaneous estimation of stable between-person differences and dynamic within-person fluctuations in a single multilevel model.
Random-intercept linear mixed-effects models were estimated using maximum likelihood with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015; Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Random-intercept linear mixed-effects models were estimated using maximum likelihood with the lme4 package <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bates et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: An unconditional null model (M0) estimated the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).

The primary analytic sequence comprised three nested models: M1 (BRI within + between + covariates), M2 (SI within + between + covariates), and M3, the main model (BRI + SI within + between + covariates).
M4 added BRI × SI interaction terms to M3.
Model fit was compared using likelihood ratio tests.

Proportional reduction in variance (PRV) was computed by comparing between-person and residual variance components from M0 and M3, both estimated using restricted maximum likelihood on the same analytic sample (Nakagawa & Schielzeth, 2013).
text.formatted: Proportional reduction in variance (PRV) was computed by comparing between-person and residual variance components from M0 and M3, both estimated using restricted maximum likelihood on the same analytic sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Nakagawa & Schielzeth, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A component-level sensitivity model (component model) replaced the BRI composite with its three standardized components.
A second sensitivity model (M5) substituted the six-item SI composite.

To evaluate whether the six-item subsample itself (rather than the SI measure) drove differences in results, M3 was also refit on the 1,048-observation six-item subsample (M3-sub), enabling a samesample comparison of M3-sub and M5.

A third sensitivity model (M6) added chronic condition count as a time-varying covariate (within-person deviation and person mean) to M3 to assess whether BRI associations with depressive symptoms were robust after accounting for physical health burden.
All analyses used R version 4.3.3 (R Core Team, 2024).
Table 1 presents descriptive characteristics of the analytic sample.
The sample was predominantly White (approximately 82%) and female (approximately 54%) across all three rounds.
Mean depressive symptom scores were 0.65 (SD = 0.96) in Round 12, 0.64 (SD = 0.94) in Round 13, and 0.67 (SD = 0.93) in Round 14.
The null-model ICC was 0.577, indicating that approximately 58% of total depressive symptom variance reflected stable between-person differences.
Table 2 presents results from the primary multilevel models.

In the main model (M3), higher BRI was independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms both between persons (B = -0.238, SE = 0.055, p < .001) and within persons (B = -0.139, SE = 0.056, p = .013).
text.formatted: In the main model (M3), higher BRI was independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms both between persons (B = -0.238, SE = 0.055, p < .001) and within persons (B = -0.139, SE = 0.056, p = .013).

text.text: Participants with higher average BRI reported fewer depressive symptoms overall; moreover, in waves when an individual's BRI was above their own mean, they tended to report fewer symptoms.
Greater between-person social interaction was also independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms (B = -0.714, SE = 0.132, p < .001).
text.formatted: Greater between-person social interaction was also independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms (B = -0.714, SE = 0.132, p < .001).

text.text: The within-person social interaction association was not statistically significant (B = 0.114, SE = 0.136, p = .403), indicating that waves with higher-than-usual social participation were not accompanied by fewer symptoms within the same individual.

Among covariates, female sex was associated with higher depressive symptom scores (B = 0.179, SE = 0.067, p = .008), and higher education was consistently associated with fewer symptoms relative to less than high school (see Table 2).
text.formatted: Among covariates, female sex was associated with higher depressive symptom scores (B = 0.179, SE = 0.067, p = .008), and higher education was consistently associated with fewer symptoms relative to less than high school (see Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Adding social interaction to the BRI-only model significantly improved fit (χ²(2) = 29.18, p < .001).
text.formatted: Adding social interaction to the BRI-only model significantly improved fit (χ²(2) = 29.18, p < .001).

text.text: Adding BRI × SI interaction terms did not improve fit (χ²(2) = 2.05, p = .359); neither the within-person interaction (B = -0.818, SE = 0.583, p = .161) nor the between-person interaction (B = 0.055, SE = 0.206, p = .789) was significant.
Relative to the null model, M3 reduced between-person variance by 16.9% and residual variance by 0.9%.
Table 3 presents results from three sensitivity analyses.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">3</ref> presents results from three sensitivity analyses.

text.text: The betweenperson BRI association remained significant (B = -0.275, SE = 0.066, p < .001).
text.formatted: The betweenperson BRI association remained significant (B = -0.275, SE = 0.066, p < .001).

text.text: The withinperson BRI association was not significant (B = -0.086, SE = 0.066, p = .198).
Between-person social interaction was significant (B = -0.807, SE = 0.173, p < .001); within-person social interaction was not (B = 0.036, SE = 0.181, p = .845).
text.formatted: Between-person social interaction was significant (B = -0.807, SE = 0.173, p < .001); within-person social interaction was not (B = 0.036, SE = 0.181, p = .845).

text.text: When the three BRI components were entered separately with social interaction and covariates, mean activity level showed the strongest independent between-person association (B = -0.179, SE = 0.038, p < .001).
text.formatted: When the three BRI components were entered separately with social interaction and covariates, mean activity level showed the strongest independent between-person association (B = -0.179, SE = 0.038, p < .001).

text.text: Between-person relative amplitude was borderline significant (B = -0.071, SE = 0.036, p = .051), and the between-person reversed CV coefficient was positive and nonsignificant (B = 0.060, SE = 0.043, p = .163).
No within-person component reached significance.
These mutually adjusted estimates reflect shared variance among correlated components and do not isolate independent causal contributions.

After adding chronic condition count as a time-varying covariate (within-person: B = 0.106, SE = 0.053, p = .048; between-person: B = 0.153, SE = 0.024, p < .001), BRI remained independently associated with depressive symptoms at both levels: within-person (B = -0.128, SE = 0.056, p = .023) and between-person (B = -0.187, SE = 0.054, p < .001).
text.formatted: After adding chronic condition count as a time-varying covariate (within-person: B = 0.106, SE = 0.053, p = .048; between-person: B = 0.153, SE = 0.024, p < .001), BRI remained independently associated with depressive symptoms at both levels: within-person (B = -0.128, SE = 0.056, p = .023) and between-person (B = -0.187, SE = 0.054, p < .001).

text.text: These findings suggest that the BRI-depressive symptom associations persisted after adjustment for chronic condition burden, although residual confounding by physical health cannot be excluded.

On the same 1,048 person-waves, the within-person BRI association with four-item SI was also nonsignificant (B = -0.083, SE = 0.066, p = .212), while the between-person association remained significant (B = -0.256, SE = 0.066, p < .001).
text.formatted: On the same 1,048 person-waves, the within-person BRI association with four-item SI was also nonsignificant (B = -0.083, SE = 0.066, p = .212), while the between-person association remained significant (B = -0.256, SE = 0.066, p < .001).

text.text: This study examined the independent associations of rest-activity rhythm organization and social interaction with depressive symptoms in community-dwelling older adults across three annual waves of NHATS.
Three findings stand out.
First, higher BRI was associated with fewer depressive symptoms both between and within individuals, though the within-person association was not robust across sensitivity analyses.
Second, greater habitual social interaction was independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms between individuals, but not within persons.
Third, no statistically significant interaction between BRI and social interaction was observed at either level of analysis.
All findings are associational; the observational design does not support causal inference.

The between-person association of BRI with depressive symptoms is consistent with social rhythm theory, which posits that stable, recurring behavioral patterns entrain circadian rhythms and support mood regulation (Ehlers et al., 1988; Frank et al., 2005).
text.formatted: The between-person association of BRI with depressive symptoms is consistent with social rhythm theory, which posits that stable, recurring behavioral patterns entrain circadian rhythms and support mood regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ehlers et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Frank et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals who maintained more active and behaviorally robust daily patterns across the three waves reported fewer depressive symptoms overall.
This is consistent with prior research linking accelerometerderived rhythm indices to depression and psychological well-being in older adults (Authors, 2026; Luik et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This is consistent with prior research linking accelerometerderived rhythm indices to depression and psychological well-being in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Authors, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Luik et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Component analyses suggest that the BRI association was most clearly driven by overall activity volume, with relative amplitude showing a borderline contribution and reversed CV contributing least independently when all three components were examined simultaneously.

The component-level findings suggest that activity volume and rhythm-related features may be difficult to disentangle within the present composite, underscoring the importance of interpreting BRI as a multidimensional behavioral measure rather than a pure indicator of circadian organization.
The within-person BRI association was significant in the primary model but did not replicate in the smaller sensitivity subsample.
This pattern warrants caution in interpretation.

Annual assessments may be too infrequent to detect shorter-term covariation between daily activity organization and mood, as fluctuations in both likely occur over days or weeks rather than years (Monk et al., 1991).
text.formatted: Annual assessments may be too infrequent to detect shorter-term covariation between daily activity organization and mood, as fluctuations in both likely occur over days or weeks rather than years <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Monk et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: The discrepancy may also reflect reduced statistical power in the sensitivity subsample (434 vs. 606 participants), as same-sample comparisons showed consistent nonsignificance once the sample was restricted.
Taken together, there is clearer evidence for a stable between-person association than for a dynamic within-person relationship at annual intervals.

The between-person association of social interaction with depressive symptoms is consistent with a substantial literature linking habitual social participation to late-life mental health (Santini et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The between-person association of social interaction with depressive symptoms is consistent with a substantial literature linking habitual social participation to late-life mental health <ref type="bibr">(Santini et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Older adults who engaged more consistently in social activities across waves reported fewer depressive symptoms, a pattern also consistent with behavioral activation theory, which posits that engagement with rewarding activities reduces depressive symptomatology through positive reinforcement and reduced rumination (Martell et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Older adults who engaged more consistently in social activities across waves reported fewer depressive symptoms, a pattern also consistent with behavioral activation theory, which posits that engagement with rewarding activities reduces depressive symptomatology through positive reinforcement and reduced rumination <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Martell et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Social activities may further buffer against depression by sustaining a sense of social identity and purpose, particularly in later life when social roles often contract (Fiske et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Social activities may further buffer against depression by sustaining a sense of social identity and purpose, particularly in later life when social roles often contract <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Fiske et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of a significant within-person social interaction association suggests that waves with higher-than-usual social participation did not coincide with fewer symptoms within the same individual.
Annual assessments likely cannot capture shorter-term fluctuations in social engagement and mood that may unfold over days or weeks.

Alternatively, the between-person association may partly reflect stable individual differences in sociability, functional status, or personality that the covariates do not fully capture, rather than a truly dynamic relationship.
These explanations are not mutually exclusive and would require more frequent longitudinal assessments to disentangle.
We found no evidence that BRI and social interaction interacted at either level of analysis.

Interaction tests are known to be underpowered in observational studies, and the within-person interaction estimate (B = -0.818, SE = 0.583) was large in magnitude with a wide confidence interval, suggesting that the null result should be interpreted cautiously rather than as evidence that the effects are independent.

This pattern is consistent with social rhythm theory's framing of social zeitgebers as one input to behavioral and circadian regulation, rather than a necessary condition for rhythm organization to be relevant to mood (Ehlers et al., 1988).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with social rhythm theory's framing of social zeitgebers as one input to behavioral and circadian regulation, rather than a necessary condition for rhythm organization to be relevant to mood <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ehlers et al., 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Strengths of this study include repeated objective accelerometer assessments across three annual waves of a large, population-based cohort, explicit within-between decomposition (Bell et al., 2019; Curran & Bauer, 2011), and sensitivity analyses testing a broader social interaction measure and individual BRI components.
text.formatted: Strengths of this study include repeated objective accelerometer assessments across three annual waves of a large, population-based cohort, explicit within-between decomposition <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Curran & Bauer, 2011)</ref>, and sensitivity analyses testing a broader social interaction measure and individual BRI components.

text.text: Limitations include: the annual assessment interval, which may be too coarse to detect within-person dynamics; the use of a NHATS-adapted 0-4 PHQ-2 scoring that departs from standard PHQ-2 conventions; and sample restriction to accelerometer participants, which limits generalizability to the broader NHATS population.
The observational design precludes causal inference.
In particular, reverse causation is plausible: depressive symptoms (psychomotor slowing, anhedonia, fatigue) may reduce activity and social engagement rather than the other way around.
Lagged models or quasi-experimental designs would be needed to address this limitation.
Future research should use ecological momentary assessment or more frequent accelerometry-linked surveys to detect shorter-term within-person dynamics.
Studies incorporating physiological measures of circadian phase would help clarify whether associations reflect endogenous circadian processes or behavioral patterns more broadly.
Intervention studies targeting daily activity organization or social participation would provide causal evidence for the relationships observed here.

In this three-wave cohort of community-dwelling older adults, more active and behaviorally robust daily patterns and greater habitual social engagement were each independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms between individuals.

To contextualize the magnitude, a 1-SD higher between-person BRI was associated with a 0.154-point lower PHQ-2 score on a 0-4 scale (between-person BRI SD = 0.647; PHQ-2 SD = 0.948), equivalent to approximately 0.16 SD in depressive symptoms-a modest association.
These findings support further investigation of behavioral rhythm organization and social participation as potentially modifiable targets relevant to late-life depression.
